name: Prevention Over Cure
description: Recognize the first useful warning of a BJJ pass, pin, or submission setup, and practice intervening while you still have space and choices to work with.
summary: Early defense addresses the grip, angle, or connection that enables a threat before the opponent completes it.
overview: When you review an escape failure, look a little earlier than the pin. There may have been a moment when your elbow could stay inside or your knee could return without first moving the opponent’s settled weight.
key_takeaways: Learn the earliest cue you can reliably recognize, such as a cleared knee or a hand entering a collar.
Prevent the next meaningful control, rather than fighting every touch as though it were equally urgent.
Keep the threatened space occupied with an appropriate frame or leg barrier while you recover your position.
If the early defense fails, acknowledge the new position and switch to a taught escape.
An immediate submission threat takes priority over stopping a positional advance.

bjj_applications.scenario: A passer clears your knee shield but has not yet settled chest-to-chest.
bjj_applications.application: Use the remaining space to restore a leg barrier or recover an inside frame. Once they settle the pin, switch to the escape that fits the controls they have established.
bjj_applications.outcome: You distinguish the chance to recover guard from the later task of escaping a pin.

bjj_applications.scenario: A partner begins feeding a collar grip toward your neck.
bjj_applications.application: Address the grip and posture before continuing your own attack. Notice what keeps the attacking hand from reaching its next useful control.
bjj_applications.outcome: You respond to the setup while it is still changing.

bjj_applications.scenario: An opponent circles behind you during a passing scramble.
bjj_applications.application: Track the loss of your ability to face them. Recover that alignment while space remains; if they establish back control, protect against the immediate attack and use your practiced back defense.
bjj_applications.outcome: You avoid treating an established back attack as though it were still only a passing problem.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to stop every grip with the same urgency.
common_mistakes.consequence: You can surrender useful position while chasing a harmless connection.
common_mistakes.correction: Ask what the grip enables and whether a more immediate threat is developing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Continuing the early defense after the opponent has already settled the pin.
common_mistakes.consequence: You may reach or twist without the space that made the original response available.
common_mistakes.correction: Recognize the changed position, rebuild your defense, and choose the appropriate escape.

common_mistakes.mistake: Practicing only from completely established bad positions.
common_mistakes.consequence: You miss the decisions that led into those positions.
common_mistakes.correction: Include starts just before the decisive grip or barrier is lost.

training_exercises.name: One step before the pin
training_exercises.description: Start with a partner passing your half guard, just before the knee shield is cleared. The passer tries to settle side control; the defender tries to restore a leg barrier. Reset on either result or a tap. Repeat from a slightly later start to identify when recovery becomes a pin-escape problem.
training_exercises.focus: Recognize the boundary between prevention and escape.

knowledge_assessment.question: What changes when the early defensive opportunity has passed?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The available space and controls have changed, so switch to defending and escaping the position that now exists.
